description: Conservators need to compare condition notes across time to determine whether subtle deterioration is real, newly emerging, or just described differently by different staff.

user_profile.persona: 41-year-old conservator used to working with gradual, ambiguous change
user_profile.context: Recent notes suggest a shift, but the evidence is dispersed across old reports and varying terminology
user_profile.communication_style: Precise and pattern-sensitive, prefers careful comparison over fast conclusions

fact_sheet.fact: The artifact in question is a Late Roman Gilt-Bronze Fibula with accession number AM-2004.11.3.
Artifact AM-2004.11.3 is currently stored in the Aethelburg Museum's Climate-Controlled Vault 2, inside custom Ethafoam mount in Drawer C-17.
The mandated environmental conditions for Vault 2 are a stable temperature of 18°C (+/- 1°C) and a relative humidity of 45% (+/- 2%).
Elena Vance is the Senior Conservator of Metals and is the primary caretaker for artifact AM-2004.11.3.
Dr. Alistair Finch, the previous conservator for this object, retired in June 2019.
Kenji Tanaka, a Conservation Technician, performed the most recent photo-documentation of the fibula on March 12, 2024.
The museum's official collection management system is ArchaiaBase v4.7, accessible at https://aethelburg.internal/archaiabase.
All digital files for artifact AM-2004.11.3, including images and reports, are stored at the network path: \\apollo\Conservation\Object_Files\Roman\AM-2004.11.3\.
A condition report from May 5, 2009, authored by Dr. Alistair Finch, describes an area on the fibula's bow as having 'minor surface pitting'.
A subsequent report from July 18, 2017, authored by Elena Vance, describes the same area on the fibula's bow using the term 'incipient delamination of the gilt layer'.
A recent technician's note added by Kenji Tanaka on March 15, 2024, describes 'a 2mm area of green, powdery efflorescence near the pin hinge'.
In 2011, a stable hairline crack on the catchplate was measured at 1.5mm in length using a measuring microscope.
On March 12, 2024, the crack on the catchplate was remeasured by Elena Vance using digital calipers and found to be 1.7mm in length.
The museum's 'Standardized Conservation Terminology Guide, v3.1' is located at \\apollo\Conservation\Protocols\Terminology_Guide.pdf.
The standard protocol for condition photography requires a 300 DPI TIFF image that includes a 6-inch scale bar and a Kodak Q-14 color chart.
Per museum policy, new condition observations must be added as new, dated entries in ArchaiaBase; previous entries are locked and cannot be edited.
Elena Vance's primary examination workstation is Bench 4 in the main conservation lab, Room 3B.
The high-resolution digital microscope is located in the Imaging Suite, Room 3C, and must be booked via the lab's shared Outlook calendar.
All hard-copy conservation reports created before the 2015 digital migration are filed in Cabinet 7, Drawer B, in the conservation office.
The software used for multispectral imaging is SpectraView Pro, installed on the dedicated PC in the Imaging Suite.
The Head of Conservation, Dr. Isolde Reyes, must approve any request for destructive analysis; her office is Room 3A.
The fibula AM-2004.11.3 was excavated from the 'Verulamium Villa Site' in 1998 by a team from the University of Northumbria.
The conservation department uses the Slack channel #conservation-lab for informal daily updates and queries.
Requests for X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis must be submitted using Form C-11 and placed in Dr. Reyes's inbox for review.
The last full conservation treatment performed on AM-2004.11.3 was a benzotriazole (BTA) coating application on June 1, 2009.
The environmental monitoring system for Vault 2, a 'DataLoggr 5000', sends an SMS alert to Elena Vance's phone if humidity deviates by more than 5% for over one hour.
